documents.title: Preventive Medicine Consultation
documents.author: preventive medicine
documents.body:
PREVENTIVE MEDICINE, EMPLOYER HEALTH SCREENING PROGRAM
Date of service: 08/14/2024
Patient: Craig Abbott, DOB 08/09/1973

Scheduled visit to go over this year's occupational screening and his heart risk.
Background: hypertension, gout, work-related noise-induced hearing loss, occupational lead poisoning in 2022 now off lead tasks.
Medications: lisinopril 10 mg daily, allopurinol 300 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.
Social: technician at a battery recycling plant. Stopped smoking 10 years ago. Alcohol socially, 2 to 3 drinks weekly.
Family: father hypertension, paternal uncle gout, mother hypothyroidism.

Screening results:
- Blood lead 16 mcg/dL, continuing to fall.
- Creatinine 1.4.
- Audiogram unchanged from 2022.
- Lipids: total 196, HDL 46, LDL 122, triglycerides 140.

Cardiovascular risk: pooled cohort 10-year ASCVD estimate 6.8% (borderline). Explained in plain numbers what that estimate means: out of 100 men like him, about 7 would be expected to have a heart attack or stroke in 10 years.
Recommendations: no statin at this time; Mediterranean-style eating, keep up cycling, limit alcohol. Continue care with primary care for blood pressure and gout. Annual screening next year.

Preventive Medicine Physician
cc: primary care

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast
reports.text:
Technique: helical CT of the abdomen and pelvis without oral or IV contrast, renal stone protocol.
Findings: 4 mm calculus in the left distal ureter about 2 cm above the ureterovesical junction, low attenuation (approximately 420 HU), not seen on the scout image. No hydronephrosis. Kidneys normal in size with no additional calculi. Right ureter and bladder unremarkable. Liver, spleen, pancreas and adrenals unremarkable. No free fluid. Appendix normal. Lung bases clear.
reports.conclusion: 4 mm left distal ureteral calculus, low density, suggestive of uric acid composition. No hydronephrosis.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT, REGIONAL HOSPITAL
Arrival 01/31/2026 09:40. Received by primary care 02/03/2026.
Pt: Craig Abbott, 52M. Allergies: NKDA.

HPI: Sharp pain in the left side that came on suddenly this morning and hasn't let up, with nausea, no vomiting. Can't get comfortable, keeps changing position on the stretcher. No injury, no recent illness. Rode an organized cycling event in hot weather last weekend on a trip south. First time with pain like this. No burning with urination, no penile discharge.
PMH: HTN, gout, occupational lead poisoning (followed by occupational medicine and PCP), noise-induced hearing loss. Meds: lisinopril 10 mg daily, allopurinol 300 mg daily.
FH: father HTN, paternal uncle gout, mother hypothyroidism.
SH: former smoker, social alcohol, battery recycling technician. Eats a lot of red meat and seafood.

Triage: HR 108, BP 166/98, afebrile, SpO2 98% RA. Pain 9/10.
Exam: uncomfortable, writhing. Left CVA tenderness. Abdomen soft, no peritoneal signs. No testicular tenderness.

UA: many RBCs (>50/hpf), pH 5.0, no bacteria, no casts, nitrite and LE negative.
Cr 1.4 (baseline per records 1.3-1.4). WBC normal. Uric acid 8.9.
CT A/P without contrast: 4 mm left distal ureteral stone, low density, no hydronephrosis.

ED course: IV fluids, IV acetaminophen, IV ondansetron. Pain improved to 5/10, recurred.
Impression: left distal ureterolithiasis, likely uric acid.
Disposition: placed in observation for pain control and stone passage; strain all urine.

medications.sig: Take 1 capsule by mouth daily for 14 days
Dissolve 1 tablet on the tongue every 8 hours as needed for nausea
Take 2 tablets by mouth every 6 hours as needed for pain

documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL, OBSERVATION UNIT
Admit 01/31/2026, discharge 02/01/2026.
Patient: Craig Abbott, DOB 08/09/1973. Allergies: NKDA.
Reason for observation: left renal colic from a 4 mm distal ureteral stone.
Course: oral fluids and IV fluids overnight, tamsulosin started, acetaminophen and ondansetron. Passed a small stone into the strainer at 05:20 on 2/1 with prompt relief. Sent for analysis. Eating and voiding normally; pain 0/10 at discharge.
Discharge diagnosis: left distal ureterolithiasis, stone passed.
Discharge medications: tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily x14 days (may stop sooner since stone passed), ondansetron 4 mg ODT q8h prn, acetaminophen 1000 mg q6h prn. Continue lisinopril 10 mg and allopurinol 300 mg.
Follow-up: primary care within 1-2 weeks; stone analysis to be forwarded.
Hospitalist

documents.title: Follow-up after ED / observation
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen in the ED 1/31 for L renal colic, observation overnight, passed a 4 mm stone 2/1. Analysis: 100% uric acid.
Feels completely fine. No flank pain, no blood in urine, no fever. Stopped tamsulosin yesterday.
Admits he eats red meat or shellfish most days and doesn't drink much water on shift. Gout: no flares.
Meds: lisinopril 10, allopurinol 300. NKDA.

Exam: BP above goal. No CVA tenderness. Abd soft, NT.
Reviewed ED labs: Cr 1.4 (his baseline), uric acid 8.9, urine pH 5.0.

A/P
1. Uric acid ureteral stone, passed. Acidic urine and uric acid above goal both favor recurrence. Start potassium citrate 10 mEq BID to bring urine pH up; he'll check urine pH strips at home, aiming for 6-6.5. Fluids at least 2.5 L/day. Cut back red meat and seafood.
2. Gout / hyperuricemia: increase allopurinol to 400 mg daily (100 mg tabs x4), target uric acid under 6.
3. HTN: on lisinopril with new potassium citrate, will check potassium and creatinine in 3 months.
4. Lead poisoning, stable.
RTC 3 months with uric acid, BMP.

3. HTN: continue lisinopril 10.

BMP, CBC, uric acid, lead. Physical in the fall.
